shipped.title_o: Skilled performance, practice, and the differentiation of speed-up from automatization effects: Evidence from second language word recognition
shipped.outcome_quote: The results of the current study supported Segalowitz and Segalowitz’ (1993) hypothesis (CV decreased as speakers developed automatic processing skills), regardless of whether the data were cleaned (see Table 4). Data cleaning did not affect overall patterns of RTs, standard deviations, and CVs in any task, yet it boosted accuracy rates and caused some contrasts that had initially been nonsignificant to become significant, notably in the semantic classification and sentence verification tasks. Thus, only after data cleaning were the intermediate learners found to retrieve word meanings with more difficulty than the native speakers (p = .009 for RTs, p = .011 for standard deviations, p = .046 for CVs). No such difference was found for the advanced learners versus the native speakers. Similarly, after data cleaning, but not before, nonnative speakers appeared to be less efficient at sentence verification than native speakers, at least when both plausible and implausible sentences were considered together. Finally, the findings of the sentence construction task seemed to be the most robust, given that CV decreased with increasing proficiency level both before and after data cleaning.
